title: The Ramayana: an Historical Study
html:
The Ramayana – An Historical Study.*

BY

MR. P. V. NANU PILLAI, B.A.

Of all the great literary productions of ancient India none is more widely popular or is more generally appreciated by Hindus of all classes and of different degrees of intelligence than the Ramayana of Valmiki. There are greater and even sublimer works, such as the Vedas and the Upanishads. But none of them except the Mahabharatha can be said to be so well-known to and appreciated by the people at large. Even the Mahabharatha is not so much an epic poem, as it is an encyclopædia of ancient Hindu legends and folklore, collected and collated by successive authors known by the general designation of Vyasa. Further it is an unwieldy work, perhaps the longest poetical work in the World. The Ramayana, on the other hand, is the work of a single author, Valmiki, justly known as the Adikavi or the first poet. He is not merely first in the order of time, but first also in the order of merit. Of all the epic poems in the world, the Ramayana stands unparalleled. Its peculiar fascination lies in the compactness of the story, in the chasteness and the simplicity of its language, in the loftiness of its ethics and above all in the religious instruction which it imparts to its votaries. The word Rama is a household name in every Hindu family. It has such significance to the Hindu mind that it is almost synonymous with the name of God—so much so that the very uttering of the word, a number of times, constitutes a round of prayer in the case of an ordinary Hindu. The word Rama is derived from the word ram which means to please, and it is used in the sense of Atmaram, i.e., that which pleases the soul.

* The Editor desires it to be understood that, in printing this paper in the Tamilian Antiquary, he does not accept any responsibility for the views expressed by the writer. The paper is reprinted by kind permission from the "Malabar Quarterly Review" only as showing the different aspects of this much-discussed question.

It is therefore no wonder, that the epic poem which celebrates the deeds of Rama has so much charm to the Hindu mind. It is to the Hindus what the Bible is to the Christians, the Koran to the Mohammadans, the Avesta to the Parsis and the Bodhisathwa to the Buddhists. The story of the Ramayana is a simple one and a brief summary of it, in as few words as possible, will be a fitting introduction to the subject of this paper, as in the course of our discussion, frequent allusion has to be made to it.

Dasaratha, king of Ayoshya, is afflicted with the sad thought that he has no son and the reflection Aputrasyagatir-nasti, “the sonless have no salvation” makes him quite miserable. With a view to beget a son to whom to bequeathe the kingdom which has had an uninterrupted line of succession, he performs a great yagam to propitiate the gods. Pleased with its austerity, they bless him with four sons. The eldest of these, born of Kausalya one of the three consorts of the king, was called Rama. The next one Bharatha, was born of Kaikeyi. Sumithra gave birth to the twins Lakshmana and Sathrughna. When Rama came of age, King Dasaratha made preparations to install him on his throne and seek rest in forest which his growing years and the custom of his country rendered necessary. Jealous of the preference shown by the Raja to the son of Kausalya, Kaikeyi demands of the King the fulfilment of a promise made by him in former days that her wishes would be gratified whatever they might be and whenever they were pressed forward. The King to whom truth is the highest law of being and justice is an application of it to human affairs, complies at once with Kaikeyi's request, to banish Rama to the forest and to install his son Bharatha instead. Thus Rama goes into the woods followed by his beloved wife Sita and his faithful brother Lakshmana. They wander in the forest from hermitage to hermitage for about ten years when they settled down near Nasik. At this time Ravana, King of Rakshasas, visits the hermitage of Rama during his absence and stealthily takes Sita into his aerial car and carries her away to Lanka. The brothers then set out from there in quest of Sita, form an alliance with Sugriva, the King of the Monkeys, get across to the island of Ceylon, engage Ravana in battle, vanquish him outright, recover Sita and return to Ayodhya where Sri-Rama was crowned as King.

The Ramayana like many other Indian epics is a story founded on solid facts of history. It is a history of the Aryan colonisation of South India. If by history is meant a correct record of the doings of the people at any period of their life, their habits, manners and customs, their mode of living, their way of fighting, the causes of their wars, the weapons they used in battles, the religions they professed, the ethics they followed and the gods they worshipped, we have in the Ramayana, copious materials which will afford a faithful history of the Indian people at a period long anterior to the Christian era.

The poem begins with the description of Ayodhya and an eulogium on Dasaratha and his ministers. The city of Ayodhya is described as being situate on the banks of the river Sarayu, studded with forts and fortresses, with towers and palaces. The city is peopled by the different orders of society, the Brahmans, the Kshathrias, the Vaisyas and the Sudras. The Brahmans were treated with the highest respect. The Kshathriyas occupied a position next in rank to the Brahmans. The Vaisyas formed a common folk. The Sudras were serfs in the employ of the other three classes. They were the descendants of the conquered aborginal races not much advanced in civilisation and were naturally treated therefore as servants. Dasaratha had eight ministers of the cabinet, all of them being Brahmans. Vasishta and Vamadeva were the foremost of them. Of the eight members, Purohita was the chief family priest and religious adviser to the king answering to the Archbishop of Canterbury. Next comes the Prathinidhi, the Ambassador; next in order is the Pradana or the Prime minister. The next is Suchina or the War minister. Then comes Manthri or the Chief Counsellor. Praswivaku or the Chief Judge of the Privy Council; Pandita the expert in Sruthis and Smrithis and Sumantharaka or the Private Secretary to the King, make up the cabinet of those days in strict conformity with the ordinance of Manu. The poet next describes the grief of Dasaratha on account of his being heirless. The next chapters deal with the birth of the children and their early training. They studied the Vedas and the Sastras before the age of sixteen. Intellectually and morally therefore they had no superiors. In physical pursuits also they were trained from their infancy. They were the sons of a king and as such they were trained in the use of swords and arrows and in all other manly exercises. In fact they did not neglect one branch of education to the detriment of the other. They bestowed the greatest attention upon the training of the body which we in these days of degeneration do not care for. They realised the principle that without a healthy body, healthy morality and healthy intellect were impossible. From these facts you will see how fallen the modern Hindus are in their notion of education.

The poet next goes on to describe the Swayamvaram of Sita, and the intrigues at the Court of Ayodhya by reason of which Rama is banished into the Dekhan which is described as a huge forest inhabited by races unfriendly to the Aryas.

Coming to the South of India, the poet brings us face to face with no less than half a dozen different varieties of humanity. First, we are introduced to Guha, who is described as the head of a nomadic race of people who lived upon the roots and fruits of the forests and upon the flesh of wild animals which they hunted. They had no houses but dwelt under the shades of trees or in temporary huts thatched with leaves. They were not unfriendly to the Aryans, but acknowledged their superiority. The depth of contempt in which these people were held by the Aryans may be seen from the fact that Bharata becomes astonished to hear that Sri-Rama shook hands with Guha. That Sri-Rama should pollute his person by the touch of an unclean Kiratha was really a matter of wonder and surprise to his brother Bharata. Going still more south into the Dekhan the poet brings to our view, the cannibal Viradha whom Rama kills. The poet gives us only one or two instances of cannibals whom Sri-Rama is said to have slain. The fact is that when the Aryan colonization of South India began, they found some places inhabited by cannibals whom they at once destroyed. Next we are introduced to the great Rakshasas and the Monkey races.

As I have already said, the story of the Ramayana is a history of the Aryan colonization of South India. Sri-Rama, though he is a single individual should not be treated as such. He is simply the representative of the Aryan people who have colonised the countries of South India as far as Nasik. To the south of Nasik lay the great Rakshasa kingdom and a little to the east was the Kingdom of the Monkeys. These Monkeys and Rakshasas should not be looked upon as quadrumana or demons. They represented the two prominent races of South India at the time of the Ramayana. The Rakshasas as their name indicates were a fierce race of people who scorned the supremacy of the Aryans and had withstood all their attempts to aryanize them through long ages. They occupied the countries to the south of Nasik on the west coast of India. This country extended up to Cape Comorin and thence to Ceylon. They were a considerably civilised people. They were armed with swords and spears. The science of archery was also known to them. But they excelled in the use of swords. They were perhaps acquainted with the sea and knew the art of navigation. Their Chief is said to have had an aerial car. They had a feudal system among themselves consisting of petty lords or generals who followed their king whenever called upon to do so. They were not illiterate. Their Chief, Ravana, is said to have been conversant with the Vedas and the Sastras. He had a fortress in his city of Lanka which is described as impregnable. He had two brothers whom he treated as his colleagues. He had his uncles also of whom we hear only in the first part of the story. They seem to have governed the country of Hindustan near Nasik; for they were the first to take the field against Rama to chastise him for the mutilation of Sūrpanakhâ. Ravana had two or three sons of whom Indrajit is the foremost. He is the eldest but in no place is he treated as the heir-apparent. He is treated rather as a favoured general. Ravana had a sister to whom is ascribed the cause of the war. She had a husband first who died; and she seems to have had children by him. But she was young and wanted to re-marry. The Rakshasa women were free to choose their husbands. As she was wandering in the outskirts of the empire she met with two handsome youths from the north; and naturally she felt an inclination towards them. But they mutilated her.

Coming next to the Monkey race as they were called, we find them to be a partially civilized people having their king, their government, their ministers and officers. They had a fort in which were the houses of their chiefs and their dependants. Their king Bâli is described as a powerful chief, who was feared by all. He is also a religious man and used to say his morning and evening prayers regularly. This king had an army which was large, but they had no weapons except clubs and sticks. They were a strong and well-built people. They had a settled system of inheritance. But they were mostly black and were, probably on that account, called Monkeys by the Aryans. They seem to have been the descendants of an Assyrian race of people who entered India at a very remote time. They were the worshippers of Surya or the Sun. Their king Bâli worshipped this deity in the morning and evening. Their other chief Sugriva is called the son of Surya and Hanuman their minister is said to have been a pupil of the same deity. These facts go to prove that they were an Assyrian colony that settled in India from time immemorial. They were a peace-loving race and were mostly vegetarians living upon fruits and roots. They had heard of the powers of the Aryanized Kshatrias and had taken to learning their language. Hanuman is described as speaking the Sanskrit language with a fluency and accent that astonished the brothers Rama and Lakshmana. They were therefore easily brought under the Aryan influence and turned out to be a great source of strength to the Aryans in the war that followed.

Now that I have given a description of the Rakshasas and the Monkeys and have made the reader understand that they were men like ourselves, let me resume the thread of my narrative. The Aryans, I have told had colonized all countries to the north of Nasik; and to the south of Nasik lay the kingdom of the Rakshasas. These Aryans were an agricultural people, and wherever they went they reclaimed forests and tilled the soil. They lived upon the milk of their cattle and the produce of their soil; occasionally they used to hunt and eat of the venison. Their chief was called Rama or Sri-Rama which name is perhaps identical with the Hali-Rama of the Mahabharata. Hali-Rama means the Rama with the plough and as such is a typical Aryan farmer. His wife was called Sita which again means a furrow and is again symbolical of Aryan agriculture. In the borders of their colony they frequently came in contact with the Rakshasas and had on one occasion maltreated their women having cut off their noses and ears. Ravana, the king of Rakshasas, was duly informed of this outrage and he soon came to chastize the enemy. He planned a novel mode of campaign. He knew the Aryans to be good archers and perhaps knew his own weakness also. He therefore called in the aid of Maricha who is described as assuming the form of a golden deer and enticing away the brothers, Rama and Lakshmana. This golden deer is again symbolical of wild cattle. Maricha collected a herd of wild cattle and let them loose on the crops of the Aryans.

Seeing that their crop was in danger of being destroyed all the male members went to the rescue of the same. In the meanwhile, Ravana and his followers entered their houses and carried away their implements of agriculture and all their women. When the male members returned home they found their homes plundered and deserted. They at once set out in search of their women and property. They first met with Jadayu who is described as a bird, but who in reality was the typical pariah slave of the period. He was not given entrance into the houses of the Aryans, but was allowed to live at a respectable distance from the residence of his lords. He lived upon the carcasses of men and animals. But with all that he was a faithful servant; and as such he did his best to save the women and property of his master. But he was no match to Ravana who at once cut him down with his sword. He just lived long enough to tell the story of the kidnapping of Sita.

Then the poet describes the search of Sita by Rama and Lakshmana. After many adventures, they meet with Hanuman, the minister of Sugriva. Sugriva was driven away from his kingdom by his brother Bâli and was living as an exile in the forest. So there was much of mutual sympathy between Rama and Sugriva. They enter into alliance as a sequel to which Bâli is killed in battle by Rama and the kingdom of Kishkindha is given over to Sugriva. Rama and Sugriva then find out the whereabouts of Sita and attempt to cross the Ocean. At this time Vibhishana, the traitor-brother of Ravana privately sees Rama and enters into a secret alliance with him.

With the powerful assistance of Sugriva and with the no less powerful support of Vibhishana, Rama crosses over to Ceylon, engages Ravana in battle, kills him and all his men and installs Vibhishana as King of the Rakshasas. Vibhishana in gratitude for his leige-lord takes Sita back and places her at his feet. After this Rama returns home and reigns as sovereign. Here ends practically the story of the Ramayana. From the account just now given you will find that by this war, the whole of South India including Ceylon was subdued by the Aryans and that these countries were in due course completely Aryanized.

I have now told you that the History of the Ramayana was the history of a war between the aryanized Kshatriyas of the North and the non-aryanized Rakshasas of the South. In this war the Rakshasa power was completely subdued, their kingdom being made tributary to the Empire of Ayodhya. The downfall of the Rakshasas was due partly to intrigues among themselves and partly to the powerful support the Aryans derived from the Assyrian inhabitants of India but mostly to the mental and moral superiority of the Aryans.

Now the question may naturally arise as to who these Rakshasas were. Were they Kshatrias? Or, as such were they a branch of the Aryan people? Did they belong to the Monkey race? Were they a separate race of people differing from all these? Are they in these days represented by any peoples of India?

For this purpose we have to draw a comparison between the races already treated of. First let us proceed with the question whether the Rakshasas were Monkeys and try to answer it.

  1. 1. The Monkeys are described as vegetarians, which the Rakshasas were not.
  2. 2. The Monkeys though they were a strong and well-built people were not as fierce and war-like as the Rakshasas.
  3. 3. The Monkeys were a peace-loving people. But the Rakshasas if they loved anything at all, loved war.

4. Hanuman and Sugriva are described as men almost resembling Monkeys. But Ravana is described as Daçahasya that is a double Panchahasya, which means broad-faced.

5. Bali and Sugriva worshipped the sun. But Ravana and his people worshipped Civa.

6. The Monkeys were not much learned as the Rakshasas. Ravana is said to be conversant with the Vedas and the Sastras.

7. The Monkeys had no weapons except clubs and stones. But the Rakshasas were skilled in the use of swords and spears. They knew also the art of archery.

8. The Monkeys lived in an inland country and were afraid of the ocean when they first saw it. The Rakshasas lived, some of them at least, beyond the ocean and knew the art of navigation.

9. The Rakshasas in spite of their being fierce were a more civilized people than the Monkeys.

10. The Monkeys had a system of inheritance which was from father to son. But the Rakshasas had no settled system. Ravana gets his kingdom not from his father who was a Brahman sage; but he inherits his kingdom through his mother's ancestors. Again Ravana's kingdom goes to his brother and not to his son.

11. Lastly nowhere is it said in the Ramayana that these two peoples were inter-related. In fact the Rakshasas despised the Monkeys as did the Kshatriyas also.

Now let us see whether these Rakshasas were Kshatriyas and as such Aryans.

1. They were like the Kshatriyas a warlike people.

2. Their women like the Kshatriyas were free to choose their husbands.

3. They like the Kshatriyas worshippped Civa. Almost all the Civa temples in Northern India are ascribed to the Prathishta of Janaka and other Kshatriya kings. The Civa temples in South India are ascribed to the Prathishta of Kara and other Rakshasas.

4. It was the custom among the ancient Kshatriyas when any family was going to become extinct, to beget children in Kshatriya women by Brahmans. This practice was followed in the case of Ravana.

5. Among the ancient Kshatriyas Polyandry and Polygamy prevailed as may be seen from the stories in the Mahabharata. The Rakshasas were also subject to this custom.

6. The Rakshasas used to do penance as did the Kshatriya kings. But when a Sudra did it, he was punished with death by Sri-Rama.

7. Again the Kshatriyas of the Mahabharata are described as having Asura blood in them. Whence did they get this Asura blood if they did not belong primarily to the Asura stock?

In all these respects the Kshatriyas and the Rakshasas agree. Let us now see wherein they differ.

1. The Kshatriyas professed caste and acknowledged the social superiority of the Brahmans which the Rakshasas did not.

2. The Kshatriyas had a fixed system of inheritance which, we have shewn, the Rakshsas had not.

3. The Kshatriyas performed yagas or Brahman rites which the Rakshasas made it a rule to obstruct.

4. The Rakshasas though they were once polyandrous and polygamous had become entirely mono-androus and monogamous at the time of the Ramayana.

These are the points of difference. But the points of agreement are more numerous and important than the points of difference which may be explained away by saying that Kshatrias had completely aryanized themselves under the moral influence of the Brahmans.

Now a theory may be formulated which I hope will explain the complete aryanisation of the Kshatrias.

The Aryan Brahmans entered India not as conquerors but as spiritual teachers. For they, even to this day, trace their descent from some spiritual Guru or Rishi. These Gurus were headed by a religious chief called Manu; and there were a number of successive Manus whose duty it was to make laws and regulations for the conduct and guidance of their followers from time to time. These laws and regulations are what are known as the Manava Dharma Sastras. The mission of the Aryans was thus at first a peaceful one. But in course of time they were forced to take up arms, just as the English merchants later on were forced to do so for their defence. These Aryans were mentally and morally the superiors of the peoples that inhabited India at that time. These latter belonged either to an earlier wave of the Aryan exodus to the south or to the kindred family of the Semitics or were probably a mixed race composed of both. But all accounts go to shew that they were a people closely allied to the Aryans. They were the worshippers of Civa and the idols and were probably divided into three orders of society but not into castes, the then orders being the king and their followers, the landlords and merchants and the serfs or servants.

It was at this juncture that the Aryas entered India just as it was when the Hindus were divided into four castes that the Mahomedans invaded the country. The Puranas and Itihasas describe the struggle that was going on for long ages between these Aryas and the non-Aryanized peoples of India.

Many of these latter were in due course completely aryanised and were called Manavas or the followers of Manu. The term Manava was at first a term of contempt applied by the natives of India to denote a follower of Manu just as the term Christian was a term of contempt applied originally by the Ancient Jews to denote a follower of Christ.

The Manavas were divided into four castes as the Brahmans, Kshatrias, Vysyas and Sudras of whom the Brahmans or Bhusuras were the descendants of those Rishis, who entered India for proselytizing, while the remaining castes were taken from society as it was then existing in India. But apart from these four castes, there remained a fifth class of people made up entirely of the natives of India who preferred to worship their own gods rather than submit to the gods of the Aryans. These people fled to the South of India and were called by the Aryas as Asuras and Rakshasas which terms originally meant only the ungodly or the infidel as opposed to the Aryas who were called the Suras, the godly or faithful people by pre-eminence.

With the advance of the Aryans and the aryanized natives southwards the Asuras also receded until at last all the plains of India and even Ceylon came into the Aryan possession. These Asuras and Rakshasas are then described as taking shelter in a place called Pâthâlam. It is from the confines of this Pathala that Malayavan the father of Kykesi is described as going out in search of a kinsman to marry his daughter. But finding none, he marries her to the Rishi Visravas by whom she gets three sons Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishna. When these princes grew up they regained their lost possession of Lanka and re-asserted their former predominance. It was to destroy this predominance that the Ramayana war was undertaken and the precautions taken by the Aryans to completely overthrow the rising Rakshasa power correspond exactly with the precautions taken by the English in order to subdue the rising Mahomedan power of Tippu.

Now one word about Pâthâla and I have done with this historical aspect. Where was this Pathala? Was it an under-ground world or was it any country in India itself? I say it is no under-ground world. It was some place in South India itself where the non-Aryanized population of India took final shelter. Let us then see what part of South India corresponds, exactly with the description of the Pathala mentioned in the Puranas.

I think that the country bounded on the east by the Western Ghats, on the north by the mountains near Nasik and on the west and south by the sea was probably the Pathala of the Puranas. The synonyms for Pathala are Adhobhuvana 'an under-ground world;' Balisatma, 'the country of Mahabali,' the Asura chief; Nagaloka 'the country of the serpents;' and Kuhara 'a cave.'

This country on the Malabar Coast which I have mentioned is the only place even now for a pursued army to take final shelter in South India. It was not known to the Aryans until a very late period. The Ramayana professes to be entirely ignorant of the countries South of Nasik. This country is called even to this day as Papa-Bhumi, 'the country of the Papis or Barbarians', by the Hindus. It is an under-ground world when looked down from the Western Ghats. It is again at the foot of the world when viewed from the hills. It is this country in which even to this day the memory of an Asura chief is cherished with joy and enthusiasm. Onam and other festive days are all in commemoration of the ideal Asura king Mahabali. In no other part of India we will find the memory of an Asura chief so much cherished. Again the Malabar Coast is the abode of serpents by pre-eminence. It is noted for the number and variety of its serpents. In no part of the world will you find serpents being worshipped as in Malabar. No other country of the world can boast of special serpent priests called Pullavars even to this day. These Pullavars are perhaps the descendants of a serpent worshipping people who were subdued by the Asuras. The present Nairs are probably the descendants of those Asura warriors who defied the power of the Aryans in the plains and who, when they found that resistance was hopeless to defend the plains, sent first their women and children into the country beyond the Ghats and stationed powerful military guards in all the passes that opened the country to the outer-world. The present Sasta temples stationed at the entrance to these passes were temples of Civa, originally established by the Asura armies for their worship. Even the “Keralolpathi” acknowledges that these Sasta temples were instituted for the purpose of preventing the influx of the Aryan Brahmans from the plains. All these facts more than bear out the truth of my statement that the country described as Pathala in the Puranas is the country of the Malabar Coast.

The long absence of the male members from home for defending their country and upholding their tradition led in due course to a system of matriarchal government of properties among these warlike Asuras which had developed into the Marumakkathayam law after the entire annihilation of the Asura forces in the battle of Lanka.

Now I have explained to you the common origin of the Rakshasas and the Kashatrias. It is my duty to prove that the commonly accepted theory that the Kshatrias were Aryans, who entered India along with the Brahmans, is a mistake. The surest test of kinship is inter-marriage. The very fact that there were from the beginning no inter-marriages between the Brahmans and the Kshatrias proves beyond the shadow of a doubt that they belonged either to two distinct races or at least to two different branches of the same race. If inter-marriage was current before the time of Manu, none of the Manus or no amount of legislation could have been able to check it. In fact legislation prohibiting inter-marriage would have been simply impossible. Again, the Vedic Brahmans never worshipped Civa. The name of Civa is not even mentioned in the oldest parts of the Vedas. The contempt in which this deity was held by the Brahmans may be seen from the fact that they even to this day do not partake of the food placed at the altar of Civa. The reason alleged for this attitude of the Brahmans is that Civa was a Brahman-killer. What does this mean? If it means anything at all, it is that Civa was a God of another religion entirely opposed to and subversive of Brahmanism.

To show the moral purpose of the Ramayana I need only point out to you the various aspects in which the several characters in it are delineated. The person of Sri-Rama is always held out as the highest type of man. Whether as a son or pupil, or as a brother or friend, or as husband or father, or as an ally or enemy, or as a king or sage in whatever aspects he is viewed the figure of Sri-Rama stands out pre-eminently as among the highest ideals of humanity. Coming to the character of Sita, she is held out as the highest ideal of womanhood. In spite of being placed in adverse circumstances, in spite of being exposed to imminent dangers, and at the sight of death, she preserves her equanimity of temper and is never swayed by any other consideration than firm devotion to her lord. As to the character of Bharata, Lakshmana and Satrughna each of them excels the other in their devotion to their brother. I shall close this aspect of the Ramayana with a quotation. When Bharata finds out in the forests Sri-Rama and compels him to return home these are the words that formed his answer:—“There is nothing greater than truth and truth should be esteemed the most esteemed of all things. The Vedas have their sole foundation on truth. Having promised obedience to my father’s commands I will never through covetousness or forgetfulness or blind ignorance break down the barrier of truth.”
lead:
The Ramayana – An Historical Study.*

BY

MR. P. V. NANU PILLAI, B.A.

Of all the great literary productions of ancient India none is more widely popular or is more generally appreciated by Hindus of all classes and of different degrees of intelligence than the Ramayana of Valmiki. There are greater and even sublimer works, such as the Vedas and the Upanishads. But none of them except the Mahabharatha can be said to be so well-known to and appreciated by the people at large. Even the Mahabharatha is not so much an epic poem, as it is an encyclopædia of ancient Hindu legends and folklore, collected and collated by successive authors known by the general designation of Vyasa. Further it is an unwieldy work, perhaps the longest poetical work in the World. The Ramayana, on the other hand, is the work of a single author, Valmiki, justly known as the Adikavi or the first poet. He is not merely first in the order of time, but first also in the order of merit. Of all the epic poems in the world, the Ramayana stands unparalleled. Its peculiar fascination lies in the compactness of the story, in the chasteness and the simplicity of its language, in the loftiness of its ethics and above all in the religious instruction which it imparts to its votaries. The word Rama is a household name in every Hindu family. It has such significance to the Hindu mind that it is almost synonymous with the name of God—so much so that the very uttering of the word, a number of times, constitutes a round of prayer in the case of an ordinary Hindu. The word Rama is derived from the word ram which means to please, and it is used in the sense of Atmaram, i.e., that which pleases the soul.

* The Editor desires it to be understood that, in printing this paper in the Tamilian Antiquary, he does not accept any responsibility for the views expressed by the writer. The paper is reprinted by kind permission from the "Malabar Quarterly Review" only as showing the different aspects of this much-discussed question.
